paras: The lynching of Charles Williams took place on the night of July 4, 1885, when twelve or fifteen men took Williams, a Black prisoner, from two constables on the road to Laurens Court House, South Carolina, and shot him to death. Williams had been arrested for an alleged attempt to "ravish" a young white girl and was protesting his innocence when he was seized. No arrests were reported, and the killing drew notice a month later when the Charleston News and Courier sent a correspondent to investigate a series of violent incidents in Laurens County.

According to an account the News and Courier had already published, Williams was identified as a man who entered a young girl's room at night, put his hand on her head and fled when she cried out. He was arrested for an alleged attempted rape, and on the night of the Fourth of July he was being taken under guard to Laurens Court House.

Constable J. A. Burdett and his assistant, Eddie Shell, were leading Williams by the rope that bound him, and Williams complained that he could hardly walk because of a beating he had received that morning. About five and a half miles from the Court House, twelve or fifteen men halted the party; the constables later testified that they did not see the men's color, and no masks were mentioned. The men took the prisoner down the road while he protested his innocence, and the constables, after hearing shots, went on to Laurens. No resistance by either the guards or the prisoner is recorded, and J. A. Rodgers later found Williams in the road, shot through the head.

Trial Justice W. B. Toddard, acting as coroner, held an inquest on July 5, hearing only Burdett, Shell and Rodgers. The evidence was not filed with the Clerk of Court until July 27, and by the time of the correspondent's letter no report had been made to the Governor. No report of an arrest, indictment or trial was found in the coverage.

The News and Courier blamed the county's lawlessness on "the inefficiency of the local authorities" and complained that official reports of murders had been "pigcon-hoiled" [pigeonholed] for weeks instead of being sent to the state. It urged Laurens voters to turn out the officials responsible and expressed confidence that the citizens and Governor Thompson would act.

The surviving coverage comes from the white press, chiefly the Abbeville Press and Banner's reprint on August 5 of the News and Courier correspondent's letter, headlined "Lack of Law in Laurens", and of the paper's editorial on it. The correspondent headed his section on the case "A Peculiar Lynching" and wrote that lynching for "attempts upon female honor is an established and approved practice in South Carolina", but that the "scent [scant] evidence" and quiet talk in this case called for "a more searching investigation". The editorial went further, giving the lynching "strong condemnation" and calling the killers "self-appointed jury and executioners" who had made no effort to establish Williams's guilt.

Other papers took up the Laurens series as a story of general lawlessness without naming Williams. The Eureka Daily Sentinel in Nevada praised the News and Courier for exposing offenders "of high social standing" and reprinted the editorial's closing paragraph, while the Carolina Spartan, reprinted in Abbeville on August 12, blamed shootings in Laurens and Lancaster on peace officers afraid to make arrests. No Black-press coverage of the killing was found.

The correspondent also reported "another side of the story" from people who knew the girl's family, who said her three older sisters were "of loose character" and suggested that Williams had mistaken her for one of them. He presented this as hearsay that "belongs to the case", against the earlier account that Williams had been identified as the intruder; neither version appears in the brief sworn testimony at the inquest.

reader.title: Lynching of Charles Williams
bases: Twelve or fifteen men took Williams, a Black prisoner accused of attempted rape, from the constables and shot him dead in the road (A1, A3).

Williams was taken from officers' custody by twelve or fifteen men and shot to death after being accused of an attempt to 'ravish' a white girl (A1); the News and Courier called the killers 'self-appointed jury and executioners' and found no hint of even an irregular trial (A3).

All the detail comes from one News and Courier correspondent's letter based on the inquest record (A1); the editorial (A3) relies on that letter, and the earlier News and Courier account it mentions was not found.
